etymology: Godly (after the manner of God) + sorrow; Paul’s phrase kata theon lupē, “sorrow according to God” (2 Cor 7:10).
biblical_def: Godly sorrow is the Spirit-wrought grief for sin as sin against God—a grief whose substance is the offense given to a holy Father, not chiefly the consequences felt by the offender. Paul sets the doctrine at its sharpest in 2 Corinthians 7:10: for godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. Two sorrows, one outcome each. Godly sorrow produces repentance unto salvation; worldly sorrow produces death. The Corinthians’ example, recalled by Paul with relief and joy, illustrates the seven marks: what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! Godly sorrow is therefore not a vague emotional sadness, not the merely regretful sense of having been caught, not the depressive self-pity of seeing one’s failure—but a substantive, carefully discriminating, repentance-producing grief at the offense given to God in particular, with its proper fruits in carefulness, clearing of oneself, indignation against the sin, fear, vehement desire after holiness, zeal for God’s honor, and just self-judgment. The grief is real, even severe; but its end is life, not death. David’s Psalm 51 is the great Old Testament case: against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight; the offense to God is the central grief, and the repentance that flows is genuine, structural, life-restoring. Peter’s tears after his denial belong to the same family; Judas’s remorse, by contrast, belongs to the worldly sorrow that worketh death. The pastor and self-examining saint are therefore to discriminate: a sorrow whose substance is offense against God will move toward repentance and life; a sorrow whose substance is mere chagrin at consequences will lead the soul, however many tears it sheds, toward the despair Judas walked into. The pastoral cure is the gospel: the same God against whom the sin was committed has provided in Christ the propitiation through which the godly-sorrowful soul finds, not death, but salvation.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines GODLY SORROW (after Paul’s usage) as sorrow for sin as offense against God, producing repentance unto salvation, in contrast to the sorrow of the world which worketh death.
webster_full: GODLY, a. — Pious; reverencing God, and his character and laws; obedient to the commands of God from love and reverence of his character; conformed to God’s law. As applied to sorrow, godly denotes sorrow felt before God for sin as offense against Him.

SORROW, n. — The uneasiness or pain of mind which is produced by the loss of any good, or of frustrated hopes of good, or expected loss of happiness; to be distinguished, in the apostle’s usage, from the godly sorrow which works repentance unto salvation.
scriptures: For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.

For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!
For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me. Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight.
And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And he went out, and wept bitterly.
corruption_summary: Godly sorrow is corrupted by the worldly-sorrow counterfeit—regret for consequences rather than grief at offense against God—and by the therapeutic register that has trained the believer to suspect all heavy sorrow over sin as unhealthy and to seek immediate consolation before the sorrow has done its repentance-producing work.
corruption_paragraphs: Worldly sorrow is the most pervasive counterfeit. The soul regrets having been caught, regrets the consequences fallen out, regrets the social or relational damage—but the regret has not actually been directed at the offense given to God in particular. The result is the appearance of repentance without the substance: tears flow, apologies are made, but the structural change that godly sorrow produces does not occur, and the same sin returns. Paul’s diagnostic is exact: godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. The cure is the recovery of the godward focus: confess the sin in its actual character as offense against God; let the grief settle on what the sin is rather than on what it cost; trust the propitiation; receive the forgiveness; and let the seven marks of 2 Corinthians 7:11 begin to work themselves out as the proper fruits.

The therapeutic register has trained the contemporary believer to suspect all heavy sorrow over sin as unhealthy and to seek immediate consolation before the sorrow has done its work. Conviction is brought to the conscience; the soul feels the weight; the response is reflexive: turn away from the heavy feeling, find comforting media, distract, self-soothe, find the friend who will reassure. The sorrow is closed off before it has had time to produce the repentance it was sent to produce. The biblical pattern is patient. The Spirit’s conviction is welcomed and sat with; the grief is felt as long as it needs to be felt; the seven marks are allowed to develop; and the consolation, when it comes, is the consolation of forgiveness applied to a soul that has actually repented rather than merely been distracted. Recover the patience under godly sorrow, and the soul recovers also the deep cleansing it works.
roots_summary: Paul’s phrase hē kata theon lupē (sorrow according to God—2 Cor 7:10) and the seven marks of 7:11 (carefulness, clearing, indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, revenge)—Spirit-wrought grief at sin as offense against God, producing repentance unto salvation.
roots_lines: Greek lupē (G3077) — grief, sorrow (2 Cor 7:10 of both godly and worldly sorrow).
Greek phrase kata theon — “according to God” (the qualifier that makes the sorrow godly).
Greek metanoia (G3341) — repentance (the fruit godly sorrow produces).
Hebrew nicham (H5162) — to be sorry, repent (the OT cousin verb).
usage: Two sorrows, two outcomes: godly sorrow worketh repentance unto salvation; the sorrow of the world worketh death.
The seven marks of 2 Cor 7:11 distinguish godly sorrow from its counterfeits: carefulness, clearing of oneself, indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, just self-judgment.
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned—David’s godward focus in Psalm 51 is the great OT case of godly sorrow.

etymology: Compound: sober (Latin sobrius, “not drunk, temperate”) + mindedness. Renders the Greek sōphron- family (sōphronē, sōphronisman) and nēphaleos, “sober, vigilant.”
biblical_def: Sober-mindedness is the regenerate state of soul that thinks clearly, judges soundly, holds the affections in check, and walks alert through a world the spirit of the age has otherwise made drunk. The Greek sōphron- family carries two cousin senses: self-controlled, of sound mind (Mark 5:15, the demoniac after deliverance was clothed, and in his right mind—sōphronounta) and discreet, prudent, sensible. The Greek nēphaleos-family adds the watchful, alert sense (1 Pet 5:8, be sober, be vigilant). Both come together in the apostolic call to sober-mindedness as a habitual Christian disposition: Paul charges Titus to teach young men likewise to be sober minded, and the older women to teach the younger to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children, to be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands. Peter sets it as the eschatological framing for prayer: the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer. 1 Timothy 3 makes sober-mindedness a qualification for elders and deacons. The biblical opposite is not merely literal drunkenness (though that is included) but the broader category of a soul whose judgment is impaired—by excess, by passion, by the inebriating spirit of the age, by the unexamined adoption of the world’s estimates of value. The sober-minded saint is therefore the believer who maintains clear judgment under cultural pressure, holds his affections in proper proportion (loving what is to be loved, in the measure it is to be loved), retains his vigilance against the adversary, prays with the alertness of one who knows the times are near. Sober-mindedness is not somberness or dourness; the same Paul who commands sober-mindedness commands also rejoice in the Lord alway. It is rather the inward clarity that holds joy and sorrow, expectation and patience, hope and vigilance in their proper places—the regenerate mind of a saint who has not been intoxicated by the air the world breathes.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SOBER-MINDED as having a sober mind; temperate; self-possessed; serious; chastened; sound of mind and judgment; not under the influence of intoxicating things or inflamed passions.
webster_full: SOBER, a. — 1. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; habitually temperate. 2. Not mad or insane; not wild, visionary, or heated with passion; having the regular exercise of cool dispassionate reason. Be sober, be vigilant (1 Pet 5:8). 3. Regular; calm; not under the influence of passion; as, sober judgment.
SOBER-MINDEDNESS, n. — Calmness; freedom from inordinate passions; habitual sobriety of mind.
scriptures: Young men likewise exhort to be sober minded.
But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
corruption_summary: Sober-mindedness is corrupted by the intoxicating spirit of the age that impairs judgment through saturation in entertainment, partisan passion, and the endless stream of stimulating inputs—and by the inverse caricature that mistakes biblical sober-mindedness for dour somberness rather than for the alert clarity that holds joy and vigilance in their proper places.
corruption_paragraphs: The intoxicating spirit of the age operates not chiefly through alcohol but through saturation: the endless scroll of stimulating inputs, the partisan passion that inflames the affections beyond what the matter actually warrants, the entertainment-shaped attention span that cannot sustain the patient work of clear judgment. The believer absorbs the saturation and brings to spiritual life the same impaired judgment he brings to his media consumption: he is reactive rather than reflective, he holds opinions with the heat the algorithm rewards, he cannot sustain sober attention to the things that most require it. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers also the disciplines that produce it: deliberate reduction of intoxicating inputs, sustained presence with the slower goods (Scripture, prayer, embodied fellowship, the long thought), and the cultivation of the inward clarity that walks alert through a drunken age.

The opposite corruption is the caricature of sober-mindedness as dour somberness—a heavy, joyless, suspicious disposition that mistakes itself for biblical seriousness. The same apostles who command sober-mindedness command rejoicing always; the Christ who is meek and lowly in heart is also the Christ at the wedding of Cana; the kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. Biblical sober-mindedness is alert clarity, not gloomy heaviness; it holds joy and vigilance, hope and patience, gladness and gravity in their proper places. The saint who has confused sober-mindedness with dourness has lost the gladness Scripture commands and produced a Christian persona that is harder than the New Testament’s pattern. Recover both: the alert clarity that judges soundly under cultural pressure, and the deep gladness in the Lord that the same Spirit who sobers the mind produces in the heart.
roots_summary: Greek sōphron-family (sōphronē, soundness of mind; sōphronousi, “in their right mind”) and nēphaleos-family (sober, vigilant)—the regenerate state of clear judgment, controlled affections, and watchful alertness amid a drunken age.
roots_lines: Greek sōphron (G4998) — of sound mind, sober-minded, prudent (Titus 1:8; 2:2, 5; 1 Tim 3:2).
Greek sōphronē (G4997) — soundness of mind, self-control (1 Tim 2:9, 15; Acts 26:25).
Greek nēphō (G3525) — to be sober, watchful (1 Pet 1:13; 4:7; 5:8; 1 Thess 5:6, 8).
Greek nēphaleos (G3524) — sober, temperate (1 Tim 3:2, 11; Titus 2:2).
usage: Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour—sober-mindedness is the alert posture against a real enemy.
Sober-mindedness is alert clarity, not dour somberness—the regenerate mind that holds joy and vigilance, gladness and gravity in their proper places.

The intoxicating spirit of the age operates by saturation; the recovery is the deliberate reduction of inflaming inputs and the cultivation of sustained sober attention to the things that most require it.

etymology: From heavy + -ness. Renders the Greek lupē, “grief, sorrow,” and katēpheia, “dejection”; and the Hebrew kābēd, “to be heavy.”
biblical_def: Heaviness in Scripture is the weighted, oppressed state of the soul under trial, sorrow, or felt withdrawal of God’s ordinary consolations—a real spiritual condition the New Testament names without embarrassment and pastors directly. Peter sets the keynote at 1 Peter 1:6: wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ. Several things stand together in the apostolic teaching. First, the heaviness is real: Peter does not pretend the saints are skipping through their trials; he names the actual weight. Second, it is for a season: the heaviness is not the saint’s permanent condition but a season under God’s appointed providence. Third, it is for trial: the heaviness is the appointed setting in which the faith is proven, refined, found at last unto praise and honor and glory at the appearing of Christ. Fourth, it coexists with deep joy: the same verse says ye greatly rejoice; the joy and the heaviness are simultaneously present, the joy being deep and structural, the heaviness being real and seasonal. Christ Himself entered heaviness in Gethsemane: he began to be sorrowful and very heavy; the writer to the Hebrews encourages saints who are in heaviness through manifold temptations with the example of the Captain of their salvation made perfect through sufferings. The biblical pastoral pattern is therefore not to deny the heaviness, not to pressure the suffering saint into a performed cheerfulness, and not to treat the heaviness as evidence of faithless weakness—but to name it as a real, seasonal, trial-purposed condition that coexists with the deep gospel-grounded joy, and to set the suffering soul under the same providence that brought the same heaviness upon the Christ who has gone through it before him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HEAVINESS as the quality of being heavy; weight; in scripture, sadness; sorrow; depression of spirits; affliction—a weighted state of soul under trial that coexists with deep joy.
webster_full: HEAVINESS, n. — 1. The pressure or weight which any body exerts upon another, in any place near the surface of the earth, by means of the power of gravitation. 2. Sadness; sorrow; grief; depression of spirits. If need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations (1 Pet 1:6). 3. That which is grievous or oppressive.
scriptures: Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season, if need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations: That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ.
And he took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and very heavy.
That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart.
...to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness.
corruption_summary: Heaviness is corrupted, in the contemporary church, by the prosperity-and-cheerfulness register that has trained the believer to perform a constant emotional buoyancy and to read his own heaviness as evidence of faithless weakness—against Peter’s explicit recognition that genuine saints are in heaviness through manifold temptations for a season.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity-and-cheerfulness register has trained the contemporary believer to perform a constant emotional buoyancy and to read the felt weight of trial as evidence of faithless weakness. The grieving saint is told to just praise through it; the depressed saint is suspected of insufficient gratitude; the heavy season is treated as a problem to be solved by attitude adjustment rather than as a real providence-appointed condition Scripture itself names. Peter refuses this. He writes to saints who are in heaviness through manifold temptations, does not embarrass them with the recognition, and instead frames the heaviness inside the structural deeper joy and the eschatological trial-purpose. The recovery is the recovery of the apostolic candor: real heaviness, named without shame; deep joy, present beneath the heaviness; trial-purpose, framing what God is doing through the season.

Christ Himself entered heaviness, and the Gospel narrative does not embarrass itself with the recognition: he began to be sorrowful and very heavy; my soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death. Paul writes of his great heaviness and continual sorrow for his Jewish kinsmen; Isaiah promises the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness—the trade is real and not the denial of the heaviness. The pastoral application is direct. Honor the heaviness of the saint who is heavy; name it without shame; set it under God’s appointed providence; do not press the sufferer into performance; preach the gospel that holds the deep joy beneath the seasonal weight; wait, with the saint, for the morning that follows the night—and meanwhile know that the same Christ who was heavy in Gethsemane is with the saint who is heavy now, having sanctified the experience by entering it before us.
roots_summary: Greek lupē (grief, sorrow), katēpheia (dejection), and the verb of Gethsemane adēmoneō (to be deeply distressed); Hebrew kābēd (to be heavy)—the real, seasonal, trial-appointed weight of soul that coexists with deep gospel-grounded joy.
roots_lines: Greek lupē (G3077) — grief, sorrow (1 Pet 1:6 of the saints in heaviness).
Greek adēmoneō (G85) — to be in heaviness, deeply distressed (Matt 26:37 of Christ in Gethsemane).
Greek katēpheia (G2726) — dejection, heaviness (Jas 4:9).
Hebrew kābēd (H3513) — to be heavy, weighty (the cognate of kabod, glory).
usage: Heaviness is real, seasonal, trial-appointed, and coexists with the deep gospel-grounded joy beneath it.
If need be, ye are in heaviness through manifold temptations—Peter names the condition without embarrassment and frames it for trial-purpose.
Prosperity-and-cheerfulness register pressures the heavy saint into performance; biblical pastoral pattern honors the heaviness and preaches the deeper joy that holds it.

etymology: From still + -ness; still from Old English stille, “motionless, at rest.” Renders the Hebrew rāpāh in the imperative harpū, “cease, be still” (Ps 46:10), and the Greek hēsuchia, “quietness, stillness.”
biblical_def: Stillness in Scripture is the active, willed, faith-grounded cessation of striving by which the soul takes its place before God and acknowledges Him as God. Psalm 46:10 is its great keynote: be still, and know that I am God. The Hebrew harpū means more sharply cease, let go, release: stop your striving, your self-defending, your frantic motion, and know the LORD as God. The stillness is therefore not passivity or inertia but the willed disengagement of the soul’s self-effort, that the soul may, in the resulting quiet, recognize and rest in the active God whose work needs no addition from us. The Psalter is saturated with the discipline: my soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him. He only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved. Isaiah names it as the very mark of strength: in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength (Isa 30:15)—and adds the rebuke, and ye would not. Christ at the storm on the lake says to the wind and the waves Peace, be still; the same Christ leads His disciples to come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while; and the wisdom of every saint who has known long providences includes the discipline of stillness in the closet, on the day, in the long season. Pastorally, stillness is the necessary practice of a regenerate soul living in an age of constant motion. The endless stimulation, the perpetual access, the cultivated impatience of contemporary life make stillness almost a foreign discipline; recovery requires deliberate practice. The cure for the noisy soul is not more noise but the willed silence in which the LORD’s voice can be recognized. Elijah on Horeb did not hear the LORD in the wind, earthquake, or fire—but in a still small voice; and the saint of every age has discovered the same: the voice that addresses him most deeply is heard in the stillness, not in the noise.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STILLNESS as freedom from noise or motion; calmness; quiet; silence; in scripture, the active cessation of the soul’s self-effort that acknowledges God as God.
webster_full: STILLNESS, n. — 1. Freedom from noise or sound; silence; as, the stillness of the night. 2. Freedom from motion; quietness; calmness; as, the stillness of the air. 3. Calmness of mind; tranquility; freedom from agitation. Be still, and know that I am God (Psa 46:10).
scriptures: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him.
...and after the fire a still small voice.
corruption_summary: Stillness is corrupted by the constant-motion register of contemporary life that has trained the soul to flee silence and dread quiet—and by the inverse mystical register that treats stillness as a self-emptying technique severed from the actual God Psalm 46 commands the soul to recognize in the silence.
corruption_paragraphs: The constant-motion register of the contemporary world has trained the soul to flee silence and dread quiet. The earbuds go in the moment the saint is alone; the screen is consulted the moment the line is slow; the next podcast queues automatically; the spaces that previously held stillness (the drive, the walk, the wait, the bath, the empty hour) have been systematically filled with stimulation. The result is a generation of believers who literally cannot be still for any length of time and who, when stillness is forced upon them by circumstance, find it intolerable and seek to escape it as quickly as possible. The discipline Psalm 46 names has therefore become both more necessary and more difficult than it was for any previous generation. Recover the practice deliberately: the daily stillness in the closet, the unfilled drive, the long walk without earbuds, the deliberate hour with God in silence—and the soul recovers also its capacity to hear what the noise had drowned.

The opposite corruption is the mystical register that treats stillness as a self-emptying technique severed from the actual God Psalm 46 commands the soul to recognize. Eastern-meditation practices and their secularized mindfulness descendants invite the believer into a stillness whose content is the emptying of all content—the bare attention to breath, the cessation of all thought, the practiced no-self. This is not the biblical stillness. Psalm 46:10 reads be still, and know that I am God: the stillness has an object, and the object is the LORD whom the soul recognizes in the resulting quiet. Biblical stillness is full, not empty: it ceases the soul’s striving precisely so that the LORD may be known in the cessation. Recover both ends. Practice the willed cessation against the constant-motion corruption, and direct the stillness toward the actual God of Psalm 46 against the mystical corruption—and the soul finds, in the recovered quiet, the still small voice that has been speaking all along.
roots_summary: Hebrew rāpāh (to cease, let go, be still—Ps 46:10’s imperative harpū) and shāqat (to be quiet); Greek hēsuchia (quietness, stillness)—the active willed cessation of the soul’s self-effort that recognizes God as God in the resulting quiet.
roots_lines: Hebrew rāpāh (H7503, hiphil harpū) — to cease, let go, be still (Ps 46:10).
Hebrew shāqat (H8252) — to be quiet, undisturbed.
Greek hēsuchia (G2271) — quietness, stillness (1 Tim 2:11-12; 2 Thess 3:12).
Greek sigē (G4602) — silence (Rev 8:1, “there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour”).
usage: Be still, and know that I am God—the stillness has an object, and the object is the LORD whom the soul recognizes in the resulting quiet.
Biblical stillness is full, not empty: it ceases the soul’s striving so the LORD may be known in the cessation.
Constant-motion culture flees stillness; mystical self-emptying severs it from God; biblical stillness is willed cessation directed toward the LORD of Psalm 46.

etymology: Peter’s phrase chara aneklalētos (1 Pet 1:8): “joy that cannot be spoken,” from chara (joy) + aneklalētos (not to be told out).
biblical_def: Joy unspeakable is Peter’s name for the gospel-wrought joy that exceeds the believer’s capacity to express it—the deep, full, glorified joy that takes hold of the soul who has come to love the unseen Christ and lays hold by faith on the salvation reserved for him. The text is 1 Peter 1:8: whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. Several things stand together. First, the object of the joy is Christ Himself—him, not chiefly His benefits, not the future inheritance considered apart from Him, but the unseen Christ whom the saints love and on whom they believe. The joy is christological at its root. Second, the means by which the joy comes is faith working through love—whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing. The saint has not seen Christ with the physical eye but loves Him; he does not now see Him but believes on Him; and out of that love-and-believing rises the joy. Third, the joy itself is named with two adjectives that mark its character: unspeakable (aneklalētos, beyond the capacity of speech to fully express) and full of glory (dedoxasmenē, already partaking of the eschatological glory). The joy is therefore not the ordinary cheerful state of a comfortable life—Peter writes to suffering saints in dispersion—but the deep gospel-wrought possession of the soul that has come to love and believe an unseen Lord and that finds, in that love and belief, a joy of a quality the language of earth cannot exhaust. Pastorally, joy unspeakable is therefore not an extraordinary mountaintop experience reserved for the unusually mature; it is the ordinary inheritance of the regenerate soul whose faith is laying hold on Christ and whose love is fastening upon Him. Where the joy is dim, the diagnostic question is not whether the saint is unspiritual but whether the love and faith are presently engaged with their proper object. Where they are, the joy follows—not always exuberant in feeling, often deep and quiet, but always exceeding the capacity of speech to express what it has come to possess.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines JOY as the passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; gladness; exultation; in scripture, especially the deep joy in Christ that exceeds the capacity of speech to express (1 Pet 1:8).
webster_full: JOY, n. — 1. The passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; that excitement of pleasurable feelings which is caused by success, good fortune, or some satisfactory event or prospect. 2. Gladness; delight; exultation; exhilaration of spirits. 3. In scripture, the spiritual joy in Christ; the joy of the Holy Ghost. Joy unspeakable and full of glory (1 Pet 1:8).
UNSPEAKABLE, a. — Not to be spoken; that cannot be uttered; that cannot be expressed in words; inexpressible.
scriptures: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.
And now come I to thee; and these things I speak in the world, that they might have my joy fulfilled in themselves.
For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith...
corruption_summary: Joy unspeakable is corrupted by the circumstance-dependent register of contemporary faith that locates joy in pleasant providences rather than in the unseen Christ—and by the manufactured emotional register of certain worship traditions that produces engineered intensity without the substantive love-and-faith engagement on which 1 Pet 1:8 grounds the joy.
corruption_paragraphs: The circumstance-dependent register locates joy in pleasant providences rather than in the unseen Christ on whom 1 Peter 1:8 anchors it. When providences are favorable, the believer is full of joy; when providences turn, the joy collapses, because its actual ground was the providence and not the Christ. Peter writes to saints in dispersion under suffering, and locates their joy precisely where their circumstances did not—in the unseen Christ whom they love and on whom they believe. The recovery is to relocate the joy at its biblical source: come to Christ Himself, love Him, believe on Him, fasten the affections on the Lamb that was slain who is worthy to receive the love and trust of the redeemed, and the joy follows, often quietly, often deeply, and held steady when providences shift.

The opposite corruption is the manufactured emotional register of certain worship traditions, which engineers an experience of joy-intensity through music, atmosphere, and crowd dynamics without the substantive love-and-faith engagement with the unseen Christ on which 1 Peter 1:8 grounds the joy. The believer mistakes the engineered lift for the apostolic joy unspeakable, identifies certain settings as where the joy is, and finds himself unable to access the joy in the closet, the ordinary day, the long providence. The biblical joy is not stage-dependent. It is the proper inward fruit of the soul’s love-and-belief encounter with the unseen Christ, and it travels with the saint into every setting in which that love and belief are engaged. Recover both ends: refuse the circumstance-dependent reading that loses the joy when providences turn, and refuse the manufactured-emotional substitution that mistakes engineered intensity for the apostolic joy itself. The joy is real, deep, full-of-glory, and beyond speech—wrought in the soul by the Spirit who points the love and faith of the saint to the unseen Christ on whom both fasten.
roots_summary: Greek chara (joy) + aneklalētos (unspeakable, beyond the capacity of speech) + dedoxasmenē (full of glory)—1 Peter 1:8’s threefold qualifier on the gospel-wrought joy of the soul who has come to love and believe the unseen Christ.
roots_lines: Greek chara (G5479) — joy, gladness (the great NT joy word).
Greek aneklalētos (G412) — unspeakable, inexpressible (1 Pet 1:8).
Greek doxazō (G1392) — to glorify, give glory; perfect passive participle in 1 Pet 1:8.
Greek agalliasis (G20) — exultation, gladness (Luke 1:14; Acts 2:46; Heb 1:9).
usage: Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory—the joy’s ground is the unseen Christ, its means is love-and-believing, its character beyond speech.
Joy unspeakable is the ordinary inheritance of the regenerate soul whose faith and love are presently engaged with their proper object, not an extraordinary mountaintop experience.
Circumstance-dependent joy collapses when providences turn; manufactured emotional joy needs the stage; biblical joy unspeakable is held in the closet, the ordinary day, the long providence.

etymology: Brotherly + love; renders the Greek philadelphia, “love of the brethren,” from philos (loving) + adelphos (brother).
biblical_def: Brotherly love is the warm, settled, practical love of the saints for one another as brothers—the love proper to the new family God has constituted in Christ, where the bond is not biological but blood-bought and the affection is not optional but commanded. The Greek philadelphia is a near-technical New Testament term: let brotherly love continue (Heb 13:1); be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another (Rom 12:10); but as touching brotherly love ye need not that I write unto you: for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another (1 Thess 4:9); add to your faith virtue... and to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity (2 Pet 1:5-7); seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently (1 Pet 1:22). Brotherly love is therefore the affectionate, practical, sustained love among Christians that springs from the recognition of shared sonship to the same Father, shared Lordship of the same Christ, shared indwelling of the same Spirit, and shared inheritance in the same kingdom. It expresses itself in hospitality (Heb 13:1-2), in burden-bearing (Gal 6:2), in mutual exhortation (Heb 3:13), in supplying one another’s needs (Acts 4:34; 1 John 3:17), in honor-preferring (Rom 12:10), in forbearance and forgiveness (Eph 4:32; Col 3:13), and in the laying down of life for the brethren in extreme cases (1 John 3:16). It is to be both fervent (1 Pet 1:22, ektenōs, stretched-out) and unfeigned (1 Pet 1:22, anupokritos, without hypocrisy)—hot in its actual warmth and pure in its genuineness, no performance and no mask. The visible and verifiable presence of brotherly love among Christians is named by Christ Himself as the credential of His disciples to the watching world: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BROTHERLY LOVE as the affection which is proper to brothers; in religion, the love which Christians ought to entertain for each other as members of the family of Christ.
webster_full: BROTHERLY, a. — 1. Pertaining to brothers; such as is natural for brothers. 2. Becoming brothers; affectionate; kind; as, brotherly love.

LOVE, n. — In a general sense, that strong affection of the mind which arises from the perception of agreeable qualities in any object, or which is excited by some good received. In a religious sense, the love which Christians bear to God and to one another as members of the family of Christ (1 John 4:7-21).
scriptures: Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another.
Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently.
By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
corruption_summary: Brotherly love is corrupted by the affinity-grouped, online-mediated, low-cost-friendly version of contemporary church life that has substituted shared interests, theological agreement, or social comfort for the cross-cultural, costly, commanded love of the brethren the New Testament describes.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary church has often substituted affinity-grouped affiliation for the New Testament’s brotherly love. Believers gather along the lines of shared age, life-stage, social class, education, political tribe, and theological niche—and within these comfortable affinities they exhibit a real but limited warmth. The New Testament’s vision is sharper. The brotherly love commanded crosses every natural human grouping precisely because the brotherhood is constituted by Christ and not by natural affinity: rich and poor, slave and free, Jew and Gentile, the educated and the unlettered, the temperamentally compatible and the temperamentally jarring are all brothers in the same family, and the brotherly love commanded extends across all the lines natural affinity would draw. Recover the doctrine, and the church recovers a love that demonstrates the gospel: the visible, cross-natural love of saints who would not otherwise be together but who love each other in Christ.

The companion corruption is the online-mediated and low-cost-friendly version that has reduced brotherly love to the digital affirmations of a Sunday community and the polite social presence of weekly attendance. The New Testament’s brotherly love is costly: it bears the burdens that take time, energy, and money to bear (Gal 6:2); it supplies the actual needs that close brothers and sisters in real distress (1 John 3:17); it lays down its life when love calls for that extremity (1 John 3:16); it forgives the actual offenses that close-up life-together inevitably produces (Eph 4:32); it forbears with the real frictions of imperfect saints in real proximity (Eph 4:2). The recovery is the recovery of embodied, costly, sustained brotherly love among the saints of one’s actual local church: bear the burdens you actually see, supply the needs you actually know of, forgive the brother who has actually offended, lay down what needs to be laid down. The credential Christ named—by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples—is given to a church living that pattern, not to one performing a digital affiliation.
roots_summary: Greek philadelphia (love of the brethren, from philos + adelphos): the affectionate, sustained, practical love of the saints for one another as the new family God has constituted in Christ.
roots_lines: Greek philadelphia (G5360) — love of the brethren (Rom 12:10; 1 Thess 4:9; Heb 13:1; 1 Pet 1:22; 2 Pet 1:7).
Greek adelphos (G80) — brother (the family-of-faith vocabulary of the NT).
Greek ektenōs (G1619) — fervently, stretched-out (1 Pet 1:22).
Greek anupokritos (G505) — unfeigned, without hypocrisy (1 Pet 1:22; Rom 12:9; 1 Tim 1:5).
usage: Let brotherly love continue—Hebrews 13:1 commands the discipline as the saint’s standing posture in the body.
Brotherly love is the credential of Christ’s disciples: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
Affinity-grouped affiliation and online-mediated friendliness substitute for the cross-natural, embodied, costly brotherly love the New Testament describes.

etymology: Holy + boldness; renders the Greek parrēsia, “all-saying, freedom of speech, frankness, boldness,” from pas (all) + rhēsis (speech).
biblical_def: Holy boldness is the Spirit-wrought, gospel-grounded freedom of speech and conduct by which the believer confesses Christ, prays at the throne, and stands in public witness without the muting fear that natural reluctance, official intimidation, and cultural hostility would otherwise impose. The Greek parrēsia—literally all-saying—is the great New Testament name for the disposition. It belongs first to prayer: seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:14-16); having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh; And having an high priest over the house of God; Let us draw near (Heb 10:19-22). The atoning work of Christ has secured for the saint a boldness of access to God that no Old Testament saint enjoyed in the same degree. It belongs second to public witness: in Acts the apostles, having tasted the boldness Christ promised His witnesses, speak with parrēsia repeatedly—and when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness (Acts 4:31). It belongs third to the day of judgment: herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world (1 John 4:17)—the saint who is loved and loves can stand before the Judgment Seat without dread. Holy boldness is therefore not a temperamental aggressiveness, not a natural extroversion deployed for kingdom purposes, but a Spirit-given freedom of soul that flows from union with Christ and confidence in His finished work. The temperamentally bold need not assume they possess it (natural boldness in the flesh is not the apostolic parrēsia); the temperamentally retiring need not assume they cannot have it (the Spirit gives boldness to those who pray for it, irrespective of temperament). The church saturated with holy boldness is the church that prays freely, witnesses confidently, and lives without the muting fear of man that would otherwise shrink her.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BOLDNESS as courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; fearlessness; in scripture, freedom of speech and confidence of access to God, secured by the atoning work of Christ.
webster_full: BOLDNESS, n. — 1. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; fearlessness. 2. Confidence; lack of restraint. 3. Freedom of speech; frankness. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace (Heb 4:16). 4. Forwardness; impudence; want of modesty (the corrupted form).
HOLY, a. — Properly, whole, entire or perfect, in a moral sense. Hence, pure in heart, temper or dispositions; free from sin and sinful affections; conformed in actions to the moral law.
scriptures: Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus.
And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness.

And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel, For which I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak.
corruption_summary: Holy boldness is corrupted, on one side, by the timidity register that has trained the contemporary believer to mute his confession under cultural pressure—and on the other by the brash-confidence counterfeit that mistakes natural aggressiveness for the Spirit-wrought freedom of speech that flows from union with Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Cultural pressure has produced a generation of believers trained to mute their confession of Christ in public. The fear of social cost, professional consequence, online pile-on, or relational friction has shrunk the apostolic parrēsia to a careful, edited, often apologetic witness that confesses only what is presently culturally acceptable. The recovery is not a temperamental adjustment—making the temperamentally shy into the temperamentally bold—but a Spirit-given gift sought in prayer. The apostles prayed for boldness (Acts 4:29: now, Lord, behold their threatenings: and grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word) and were given it; Paul asked the Ephesians to pray that he might speak boldly even from his bonds (Eph 6:19); the church saturated in such prayer is the church given the boldness her testimony requires.

The opposite corruption is the brash-confidence counterfeit, in which natural aggressiveness, online combat-instincts, or temperamental directness are mistaken for the Spirit-wrought parrēsia. The believer becomes loud, contentious, eager for the fight, ready to clip and post and contend, and identifies the resulting cultural-warrior persona with apostolic boldness. The two are not the same. Apostolic boldness is paired with the Spirit’s love and the wisdom from above; it is not the same as raw aggression; it does not despise meekness, gentleness, and the readiness to suffer rather than to inflict; it speaks the truth in love and bears reproach without retaliation. Recover both ends. Refuse the timidity that mutes the confession, and refuse the brash-confidence that mistakes flesh-boldness for the Spirit-wrought freedom. The biblical holy boldness is freedom-of-speech grounded in union with Christ, sought in prayer, deployed in confession and intercession, and married to the Christ-shaped love and meekness that earn the boldness its proper hearing.
roots_summary: Greek parrēsia (literally all-saying; freedom of speech, boldness, frankness)—the Spirit-given freedom of soul by which the believer prays at the throne, confesses Christ publicly, and stands without the muting fear that natural reluctance, official intimidation, and cultural hostility would impose.
roots_lines: Greek parrēsia (G3954) — all-saying, freedom of speech, boldness, frankness (31 occurrences across Acts and the Epistles).
Greek parrēsiazōmai (G3955) — to speak boldly, openly (Acts 9:27-28; 13:46; 14:3; 18:26; 19:8; 26:26).
Greek tolmáō (G5111) — to dare, to be bold (the cousin verb).
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, courageous (the OT cousin of boldness).
usage: Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace—the atoning work of Christ has secured a boldness of access to God no Old Testament saint enjoyed in the same degree.
Apostolic boldness is sought in prayer (Acts 4:29) and given by the Spirit (Acts 4:31), not produced by temperamental aggressiveness or natural extroversion.
Timidity mutes the confession; brash-confidence counterfeits the gift; biblical holy boldness is Spirit-wrought freedom paired with Christ-shaped love and meekness.

etymology: Latin fervor, “heat, boiling,” from fervere (to boil). Renders the Greek zeō (to boil; Acts 18:25, Rom 12:11) and ektenos-family (stretched-out, intense).
biblical_def: Fervor in Scripture is the boiling heat of soul—the spiritual warmth, intensity, and active energy that mark a saint truly engaged with God, the gospel, and the work of the kingdom. The Greek zeō means literally to boil; fervent in spirit in Romans 12:11 is tōi pneumati zeontes—boiling in spirit. Apollos is described as fervent in the spirit (Acts 18:25)—the same word; he taught the things of the Lord diligently, knowing only the baptism of John, but with a boiling spiritual energy that subsequent instruction by Aquila and Priscilla shaped into more accurate doctrine without dampening the fervor. James 5:16 names the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man as availing much—the fervent there carries the same boiling-heat picture. The biblical pattern therefore distinguishes fervor from two cousins. It is not the same as natural temperamental enthusiasm: the placid temperament can be no less fervent than the volatile, because biblical fervor is Spirit-wrought heat of soul, not personality. And it is not the same as unaccompanied emotional intensity: Apollos was fervent and yet teachable; biblical fervor is paired with sound doctrine, careful instruction, and ordered church life, and is not the wild-eyed enthusiasm that disdains discipline. Fervor finds its proper exercise across the Christian life: fervent love (1 Pet 4:8, charity which shall cover the multitude of sins); fervent prayer (Col 4:12 of Epaphras laboring fervently in prayers for the Colossians); fervent service (Rom 12:11 not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord); fervent zeal (2 Cor 7:11 of the Corinthians’ godly-sorrow zeal); and the fervent expectation of Christ’s coming (2 Pet 3:12 of the saints looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of God—haste there is cousin to fervor). The opposite of fervor is the lukewarmness Christ rebukes in Laodicea (Rev 3:15-16): I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot... So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth. The diagnostic of the church and saint is therefore not chiefly doctrinal precision alone (necessary as that is), nor outward activity alone (visible as that is), but the temperature of the soul: cold, lukewarm, or boiling. Fervor recovered is the soul recovering its proper Spirit-wrought heat under the Christ who Himself is the consuming fire and the giver of His Spirit who is Himself a fire.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FERVOR as heat or warmth; in a metaphorical sense, ardor of mind; warmth, eagerness, animation; intensity of feeling; in scripture, the boiling heat of spirit that marks a saint actively engaged with God and the kingdom.
webster_full: FERVOR, n. — 1. Heat or warmth; as the fervor of a summer sun. 2. Ardor of mind; warmth, eagerness, animation; intensity of feeling; as, religious fervor. Fervent in spirit; serving the Lord (Rom 12:11).
FERVENT, a. — 1. Hot; boiling; as a fervent heat. 2. Ardent; very warm; very earnest; full of intense feeling; as fervent love, fervent prayer.
scriptures: Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord.
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John.
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
corruption_summary: Fervor is corrupted by the Laodicean lukewarmness of much of the contemporary church—outward activity without inward heat, doctrinal precision without spiritual temperature—and by the inverse caricature that mistakes natural emotional volatility for the Spirit-wrought boiling-heat of soul Scripture commends.
corruption_paragraphs: The Laodicean lukewarmness Christ diagnoses in Revelation 3 is the most pastorally pressing contemporary corruption of fervor. Outward activity is sustained, doctrinal precision is maintained, attendance is recorded, programs are run—but the inward temperature of the soul is neither cold nor hot, and Christ’s verdict on the condition is sharp. The recovery is the Spirit’s work, not human energy: the heat that boiling-in-spirit names is Spirit-wrought, not flesh-produced. But the saint cooperates with the Spirit’s work by drawing near to the means by which the heat is normally given: sustained encounter with the actual Christ in the Word, prayer that lingers long enough for the heat to catch, worship that engages the affections as well as the mind, the company of fervent saints whose own fire helps to kindle one’s own. Identify the lukewarmness, refuse to accept it as the mature state, ask Christ for the recovery of the fervor He Himself commands.

The opposite corruption is the natural-temperamental version that mistakes emotional volatility for biblical fervor. The believer who is by temperament loud, intense, easily moved confuses his temperamental register with the Spirit-wrought boiling heat, and the placid believer who is by temperament steady, quiet, even-keel concludes that fervor is not for him. Both miss the doctrine. Apollos was fervent in spirit while also being instructable by Aquila and Priscilla; Epaphras labored fervently in prayer without the visible histrionics of natural intensity; the apostle Paul is described nowhere as temperamentally exuberant but as fervently engaged in the gospel across every adversity. Biblical fervor is Spirit-wrought heat of soul, not personality: any temperament can possess it, and any temperament can lack it. Recover both ends: refuse the Laodicean acceptance of lukewarmness as maturity, and refuse the confusion of fervor with natural emotional register. The boiling heat Romans 12:11 commands is available to every saint who will seek it, in the temperament he has, from the Spirit who gives it to those who ask.
roots_summary: Greek zeō (to boil—Rom 12:11, Acts 18:25), ektenos / ektenōs (stretched-out, fervent—1 Pet 1:22; 4:8; James 5:16); the Spirit-wrought boiling heat of soul, set against the Laodicean lukewarmness Christ rebukes.
roots_lines: Greek zeō (G2204) — to boil (used figuratively of spiritual fervor in Rom 12:11; Acts 18:25).
Greek ektenōs (G1619) — fervently, stretched-out (1 Pet 1:22; 4:8; Acts 12:5).
Greek ektenēs (G1618) — fervent (James 5:16, the effectual fervent prayer).
Greek chliaros (G5513) — lukewarm (Rev 3:16; the antitype of fervor).
usage: Fervent in spirit; serving the Lord—Romans 12:11’s boiling-in-spirit names the Spirit-wrought temperature of soul that marks engaged Christian service.
The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much—fervor is a quality of prayer as well as of soul.

Laodicean lukewarmness is the most pressing contemporary corruption; natural-temperamental volatility is its inverse counterfeit. Spirit-wrought heat is available to every temperament that will seek it.

etymology: Zeal from Greek zēlos, “ardor, fervor, zeal,” from zeō (to boil); of God as objective or qualifying genitive. The phrase carries two distinct biblical senses: zeal that is of God in its origin and right ordering (the Christian virtue), and zeal that is for God but not according to knowledge (the Romans 10:2 indictment).
biblical_def: The Bible uses zeal of God in two carefully distinguished senses, and the New Testament insists upon the distinction. First, there is true zeal—the Spirit-wrought, knowledge-grounded, gospel-shaped ardor for God, His honor, His Christ, His Word, His kingdom, and His holiness, that the prophets and apostles uniformly commend. Phinehas at Baal-peor was zealous with God’s own zeal and turned away wrath from Israel (Num 25:11-13); Elijah was very jealous for the LORD God of hosts; Christ at the cleansing of the temple was remembered to fulfill the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up (Ps 69:9, applied in John 2:17); the Corinthians, in their godly sorrow, demonstrated zeal as one of its seven marks; Titus is commanded to teach the redeemed people that they should be zealous of good works; the church in Laodicea is rebuked precisely for the absence of zeal—be zealous therefore, and repent. Second, there is misdirected zeal—real ardor and intensity directed at the right object but informed by wrong knowledge, with disastrous results. Paul’s diagnosis of his unbelieving Jewish kinsmen in Romans 10:2 is the textbook case: for I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. Their zeal was real, even intense; its object was God; but the knowledge informing it was deficient (they were ignorant of God’s righteousness in Christ), and the result was that their zeal drove them away from God’s actual provision rather than toward it. Paul knew this case from inside: before his conversion he had been zealous for the traditions of his fathers, persecuting the church beyond measure, thinking that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth—real zeal, wrong knowledge, deadly fruit. The biblical pattern is therefore that true zeal must be both of God (Spirit-wrought, anchored in genuine love for God) and according to knowledge (informed by sound doctrine, especially the gospel of Christ). Either side without the other goes wrong: cold doctrinal precision without ardor produces a lukewarm orthodoxy that is also rebuked; ardent zeal without sound knowledge produces fanaticism, persecution, and the missing of Christ Himself.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ZEAL as passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in scripture, the ardor for God and His glory that, when according to knowledge, is commended, but when ignorant of God’s righteousness in Christ, drives away from the very God it pursues.
webster_full: ZEAL, n. — Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing. In general, zeal is an eagerness of desire to accomplish or obtain some object, and it may be manifested either in favor of any person or thing, or in opposition to it. It is often used in a good sense, but it may be a blind, intemperate ardor. They have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge (Rom 10:2).
ZEALOUS, a. — 1. Warmly engaged or ardent in the pursuit of an object. 2. Filled with passionate ardor; full of zeal.
scriptures: For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.

Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, hath turned my wrath away from the children of Israel, while he was zealous for my sake among them, that I consumed not the children of Israel in my jealousy.
And his disciples remembered that it was written, The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.
corruption_summary: The zeal of God is corrupted, on one side, by the lukewarm-orthodoxy of churches that have retained doctrinal precision without the ardor God requires—and on the other by the zealous-ignorance Paul indicts in Romans 10:2, the real fervor for God paired with insufficient knowledge of His righteousness in Christ, driving the zealous away from the very God they pursue.
corruption_paragraphs: Lukewarm orthodoxy is the more comfortable corruption. The church retains its doctrinal precision, its careful confessions, its historical creeds, its sound preaching—and lacks the ardor Christ explicitly commands. Christ’s rebuke of the Ephesian church is the textbook diagnosis: I know thy works, and thy labour, and thy patience, and how thou canst not bear them which are evil... Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love. Doctrinal precision without the corresponding ardor is not the mature form of orthodoxy; it is its diseased form, and Christ’s warning to Ephesus (repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent) is severe. The recovery is to ask, with the kindling of fervor: where has the ardor gone, what would recover it, how is the saint to seek again the boiling-in-spirit that should accompany the careful doctrine?

Zealous ignorance is the more visible contemporary corruption—and the more dangerous, because of how confident it feels. Paul’s diagnosis of his Jewish kinsmen in Romans 10:2 applies to many religious projects across history: real ardor for God, real intensity, real sacrifice and discipline, but a deficient knowledge of God’s righteousness in Christ such that the zeal drives the zealous away from God’s actual provision rather than toward it. The cure is not the dampening of zeal but the supply of knowledge: bring the zeal under the discipline of sound doctrine, and especially under the gospel of Christ’s righteousness imputed to the believer through faith alone. Zeal informed by gospel-knowledge is the biblical virtue; zeal ignorant of the gospel is, however sincere, deadly. Recover both ends: ardor where it has cooled, knowledge where it has been insufficient—and the zeal of God in the saint becomes what Scripture commends rather than what it indicts.
roots_summary: Greek zēlos (zeal, ardor, jealousy)—a verb-cousin of zeō (to boil)—and Hebrew qin’āh (zeal, jealousy); the Spirit-wrought ardor for God that must be both of God in origin and according to knowledge in informed direction, against the two corruptions of lukewarm orthodoxy and zealous ignorance.
roots_lines: Greek zēlos (G2205) — zeal, ardor, jealousy.
Greek zēlotēs (G2207) — zealot, zealous person (the Zealots of Acts; Simon the Zealot).
Hebrew qin’āh (H7068) — jealousy, zeal (Num 25:11 of Phinehas; Ps 69:9 of the temple).
Greek zeō (G2204) — to boil (the etymological cousin of zeal-fervor).
usage: They have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge—the Romans 10:2 indictment names the real-ardor-wrong-knowledge corruption.
Phinehas, Elijah, and Christ at the temple cleansing exemplify true zeal: Spirit-wrought, knowledge-grounded, ordered to God’s honor.
Lukewarm orthodoxy retains doctrine and loses ardor; zealous ignorance retains ardor and loses gospel-knowledge; biblical zeal of God has both.

etymology: From steady + -ness; steady from Old English stede, “place, position.” Renders the Greek hedraios, “seated, settled, steadfast” (1 Cor 15:58; 7:37; Col 1:23), and ametákinētos, “unmoveable.”
biblical_def: Steadiness is the settled, unmoveable, persevering character of the regenerate soul whose foundations have been laid in Christ and whose course through life proceeds without the lurching from emphasis to emphasis, opinion to opinion, fervor to lukewarmness, that marks the unsettled believer. Paul’s great closing line of 1 Corinthians 15 gathers the doctrine: therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. Three terms stand together: stedfast (hedraioi, seated, well-anchored), unmoveable (ametákinētoi, not to be shifted), and always abounding—a steadiness that is not stagnation but the abundance-overflow of a fixed and ordered life. Paul commends Timothy similarly: but continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of (2 Tim 3:14)—the steadiness of holding fast what has been received against the constant ecclesial and cultural pressure to drift, novel, or shift. James warns of its opposite: a double minded man is unstable in all his ways. Hebrews names the steadiness of the saint’s anchored hope: which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast (Heb 6:19). The biblical pattern of steadiness has its marks. It is doctrinal: the saint continues in the things he has learned, refuses to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, holds the apostolic deposit faithfully across the years. It is practical: the saint maintains his ordinary disciplines (Word, prayer, gathering, generosity, mortification of sin, exercise of the gifts) across the seasons of life rather than abandoning them at the first cooling. It is emotional: the saint, like the Psalmist, refuses to let his soul be carried up and down by every providential gust, anchored as he is in the unchanging God. And it is moral: the saint walks the same line of integrity at sixty that he walked at thirty, with the inevitable refinement of years adding consistency rather than introducing radical course-changes. Steadiness is therefore not the same as stiffness or rigidity; the steady saint can be supple where Scripture is silent, charitable across secondary differences, growing in grace and knowledge across the years. But on the things Scripture has fixed, the steady saint is unmoveable—and that unmoveableness is the great pastoral and ecclesial gift of the long-faithful Christian to the church and to the watching world.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STEADINESS as the quality of being firm in standing or position; stability; the state of being constant in purpose or pursuit; firmness of mind or purpose; in scripture, the settled, unmoveable, persevering character of the regenerate soul anchored in Christ.
webster_full: STEADINESS, n. — 1. Firmness of standing or position; a state of being not tottering or easily moved; as the steadiness of a tower. 2. The state of being not subject to change; constancy in purpose or pursuit; perseverance. 3. Firmness of mind or purpose; resolution. 4. Constancy; consistency in moral or religious conduct.
STEADY, a. — Firm in standing or position; fixed; not tottering or shaking; stable. Be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord (1 Cor 15:58).
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil.
But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed... A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard...
corruption_summary: Steadiness is corrupted, on one side, by the novelty-chasing register that prizes the new emphasis, the new conference, the new technique, and lurches from focus to focus without settling into the long faithfulness Scripture commends—and on the other by the rigidity-caricature that mistakes mere stiffness for biblical steadiness and refuses growth in grace and knowledge along the way.
corruption_paragraphs: The novelty-chasing register is the more visible contemporary corruption. The believer moves from the latest book to the latest podcast to the latest conference to the latest movement, never settling into the patient discipline of holding what has been received and walking the long, ordinary line of faithfulness across the years. Each new emphasis is taken up with enthusiasm, then dropped for the next; the long disciplines (Word, prayer, gathering, generosity) are abandoned when they become routine; the saint reaches sixty with no greater steadiness than he had at thirty, only more bookshelves of dropped enthusiasms. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers the dignity of the long-faithful Christian: continuing in the things which he has learned and has been assured of, anchored in the unchanging gospel, refusing to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, settling into the patient course that abounds across decades.

The opposite corruption is the rigidity-caricature that mistakes mere stiffness for biblical steadiness. The believer refuses to grow in grace and knowledge, refuses to recognize legitimate development of his understanding across the years, refuses to extend charity where Scripture extends it, refuses to soften where Scripture is silent. He calls his rigidity steadiness; Scripture calls it something else. Biblical steadiness is settled on the things Scripture has fixed and supple on the things Scripture has left to liberty; it grows in grace and knowledge across the years; it extends charity across secondary differences; it is the unmoveableness of the well-anchored ship at sea, not the inflexibility of the dead tree on the hill. Recover both ends. Refuse the novelty-chasing that never settles, and refuse the rigidity that mistakes itself for fidelity. The biblical pattern is anchored and growing, settled and supple, faithful across decades and charitable across differences—and the church saturated with such steady saints is the church Scripture commends and the world quietly notices.
roots_summary: Greek hedraios (seated, settled, steadfast—1 Cor 15:58; 7:37; Col 1:23) and ametákinētos (unmoveable); the settled, unmoveable, persevering character of the regenerate soul anchored in Christ across the years.
roots_lines: Greek hedraios (G1476) — seated, settled, steadfast (1 Cor 7:37; 15:58; Col 1:23).
Greek ametákinētos (G277) — unmoveable (1 Cor 15:58).
Greek bebaios (G949) — firm, sure, steadfast (Heb 6:19, the anchor sure and stedfast).
Greek aklīnēs (G186) — not inclining, unwavering (Heb 10:23).
usage: Be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord—the three terms stand together: settled, unmoveable, abundantly fruitful.
Biblical steadiness is anchored and growing, settled and supple—not the stagnant rigidity that refuses growth in grace and knowledge.
Novelty-chasing prizes the latest emphasis; rigidity-caricature refuses growth; biblical steadiness is long faithfulness anchored in the gospel and supple where Scripture is silent.
